title: Clone Graph
description: Brute force to optimized: cloning fresh every time (broken on cycles) versus a hash map tracking original-to-clone mappings.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given a reference to a node in a connected undirected graph, return a deep copy (clone) of the entire graph: new node objects, with the exact same values and connection structure as the original.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","a reference node in the original graph"],["Output","A reference node in a completely new, deep-copied graph"],["Key Insight","A hash map from original node to its clone avoids creating duplicate clones and correctly handles cycles"],["Constraints","Up to 100 nodes"]]}

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Deep copy a graph, which may contain cycles\"","A DFS or BFS traversal combined with a hash map tracking already-cloned nodes, essential for correctly handling cycles without infinite recursion"]]}

blocks.text: Since the graph is undirected (and may contain cycles, since it is "connected", not necessarily acyclic), naively cloning a node every single time it is encountered would create duplicate clones for the same original node, and could recurse infinitely around a cycle. Maintaining a hash map from EACH original node to its (single) corresponding clone ensures a node is cloned exactly once, and subsequent encounters simply reuse the already-created clone.

blocks.title: Analogy: Photocopying a Circular Organizational Chart Without Duplicating Anyone
blocks.text: Picture photocopying an organizational chart where some reporting relationships loop back around. Keeping a running list of "who has already been photocopied" ensures each person appears exactly once in the copy, even when the chart is traversed in a way that would otherwise revisit the same person multiple times.

blocks.caption: Map original nodes to their clones; create a clone the first time a node is seen, reuse it on repeat visits

blocks.text: Cloned adjacency list: [[2,4],[1,3],[2,4],[1,3]], an exact structural match, but every node is a genuinely NEW object.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A hash map keyed by ORIGINAL node (or its value, since values are unique here) tracks which nodes have already been cloned, and what their clone is.

Observation 2: A DFS (or BFS) starting from the given node checks this map FIRST: if the current node is already mapped, its existing clone is simply reused, avoiding both duplicate work and infinite loops around cycles.

Observation 3: If the current node has NOT yet been cloned, create a new clone node immediately, and store it in the map BEFORE recursing into its neighbors (this is essential, since a neighbor might point back to this very node, and the map entry must already exist to correctly break that cycle).

Observation 4: For each neighbor of the current node, recursively clone it (or reuse its existing clone) and attach it to the current clone's neighbor list.
This leads to a DFS (or BFS) combined with a hash map from original nodes to their clones, checked before creating any new clone.
Conceptually, clone a node fresh every single time it is encountered during traversal, without tracking already-created clones.
Why the code is written this way

items: Cloning directly during traversal seems like the natural, direct approach.
Without tracking already-created clones, this creates duplicate clone objects for the same node and causes INFINITE recursion on any cycle, an actual correctness bug, not just an inefficiency.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: potentially infinite (never terminates) on a graph containing a cycle.
Space: unbounded recursion depth on a cycle.
Limitation: a hash map from original nodes to their clones, checked BEFORE creating a new clone, correctly handles cycles and avoids duplicate cloning entirely.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Maintain a hash map from original node references to their clone. Define clone(node): if node is already in the map, return its existing clone immediately. Otherwise, create a new clone with the same value, IMMEDIATELY store it in the map (before recursing further), then for every neighbor of the original node, recursively clone (or reuse) it and append it to the new clone's neighbor list. Return the clone.
Use a hash map from original nodes to their clones, checked before creating any new clone, to correctly handle cycles.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Action"],"rows":[["Visit node 1","Not in map, create clone1, store in map, recurse into neighbors 2 and 4"],["Visit node 2","Not in map, create clone2, store in map, recurse into neighbors 1 and 3"],["Node 2 recursing into 1","Already in map, REUSE clone1 directly, no infinite loop"]]}

blocks.text: Storing the newly created clone in the map IMMEDIATELY, before recursing into its neighbors, is the critical detail that correctly handles cycles: if a neighbor eventually points back to the current node (directly or through further neighbors), that recursive call finds the ALREADY-CREATED (though not yet fully populated) clone in the map and simply returns it, breaking the cycle instead of recursing infinitely; every distinct original node is cloned exactly once, guaranteed by checking the map first.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(nodes plus edges).
Space: O(nodes) for the map, plus recursion depth.

blocks.text: Clone Graph is the foundational "deep copy with cycles" problem: a hash map tracking already-cloned nodes is not an optimization here, it is a correctness requirement.

items: Storing the new clone in the map AFTER recursing into its neighbors instead of BEFORE, which fails to break cycles correctly.
Using node VALUES as the map key when values might not be unique in a more general version of this problem (though the standard version guarantees unique values).

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["A single node with no neighbors","Clone just that one node, with an empty neighbor list."],["An empty graph (node is null)","Return null directly."]]}

blocks.text: Explicitly stating "store the clone in the map before recursing into neighbors, this is what correctly handles cycles" demonstrates understanding of the critical correctness detail, not just the general DFS/BFS idea.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "deep copy a graph that may contain cycles", think: DFS/BFS with a hash map from original nodes to their clones, checked before creating a new clone.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The naive clone-every-time approach is actually broken (infinite recursion) on cyclic graphs; the hash-map approach costs O(nodes plus edges), the standard correct and efficient solution.

items: Pattern: DFS or BFS combined with a hash map tracking original-to-clone mappings.
Core Idea: create and store a clone in the map BEFORE recursing into its neighbors, correctly breaking cycles.
Time: infinite on any cycle for the naive approach, O(nodes plus edges) for the hash-map approach.
Space: unbounded for the naive approach, O(nodes) for the hash-map approach.
Most Important Observation: the hash map is a correctness requirement here (handling cycles), not merely a performance optimization.
Interview Difficulty: a classic, foundational medium-level graph traversal problem.
One line memory trick: map original to clone, check before creating.
